summary: For ages 7–9, learners meet the Inuit (Canada, Alaska, Greenland) and Sámi (northern Norway, Sweden and Finland, and Russia's Kola Peninsula) as living, present-day Arctic peoples who developed sophisticated, tested environmental knowledge. The core learning is recognising specific cultural items — parka, kayak, dog sled, igloo — and the cold or transport problem each solves, mirroring the 'same problem, clever solution' lens used for polar animals, while emphasising respect and sustainable use of animals and correct naming. A curated illustrated contemporary scene leads; in-role dialogue, matching, and build/pack tasks are offered as alternatives with distinct purposes and authenticity cautions.
misconceptions: Inuit and Sámi are peoples of the past — they are living cultures today with modern technology as well as tradition
Everyone in the Arctic lives in igloos year-round — igloos are temporary hunting/travel shelters, not permanent homes
'Eskimo' is the correct name — Inuit is the accurate term for these peoples
They survive by luck or toughness alone — they hold sophisticated, tested environmental knowledge
Using animals for food and clothing shows no care — these cultures emphasise respect and sustainable use

activities.title: Tap the Arctic scene: match each item to the problem it solves
steps: Explore an illustrated present-day Arctic scene showing an Inuit family on the sea ice and, across a ridge, a Sámi reindeer herder.
Tap the parka to reveal caribou/sealskin layers that trap warm air; say what cold problem it solves.
Tap the kayak to see it glide out to hunt on open water; say what transport problem it solves.
Tap the dog sled to watch it run across ice where wheels could not grip.
Open a cutaway of the igloo showing snow-block dome walls and a raised sleeping platform sitting above the pooled cold air, with the note 'a temporary shelter, not a year-round home'.
Lift a flap asking 'How did people learn to live here?' and read that it was generations of tested knowledge and respect for the animals they depend on.
activities.insight: These contemporary peoples solved the same cold and transport problems as polar animals — through brilliant, hard-won environmental knowledge — and they are here, thriving, today; the igloo is a temporary shelter, not a permanent home.

activities.title: Talk with an Arctic guide about living knowledge
steps: Hold a spoken or written exchange in role with an Inuit or Sámi guide about how they read the ice, herd reindeer, or build a snow shelter.
Ask the guide at least one question about how they know a particular thing (e.g. how they tell safe ice, or how snow-block walls keep warmth in).
Respond to the guide's account by naming one piece of knowledge or skill and the problem it addresses.
activities.insight: Survival in the Arctic rests on sophisticated, present-day expertise and respect for animals and land, not on luck or a vanished past.

activities.title: Build-an-igloo or pack-a-sled problem-solving task
steps: Work through a guided task to assemble an igloo from snow blocks (dome walls, raised sleeping platform above the cold-air sink) or to pack a sled for a journey across ice.
At each step, state the cold or transport problem that choice solves.
activities.insight: Each design choice is a deliberate solution to a real environmental problem — the insulating snow-block dome keeps in warmth from people and lamps, the raised platform keeps sleepers above pooled cold air, the sled carries loads where wheels fail.

activities.title: Match items to purposes (recall check)
steps: Match each Arctic item (parka, kayak, dog sled, igloo) to the problem it solves.
Then, in your own words, explain one of the matches rather than only selecting it.
activities.insight: Confirms the learner can recall which item addresses which cold or transport problem, as a stepping stone to appreciating the knowledge behind them.

checkQuestion: The Inuit (in Canada, Alaska and Greenland) and the Sami (in northern Scandinavia) have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years. A student says 'those were people from long ago who lived in igloos all the time — they don't really exist any more.' Is that right about the Inuit and Sami today, and how did knowing their environment so well help them live in the Arctic?
checkAnswer: No — the Inuit and Sami are living peoples TODAY, not just people of the past; many still keep their languages and traditions while also living modern lives. Traditionally they survived through deep, hard-won knowledge of their environment: using dog sleds and kayaks to travel, wearing warm animal-skin clothing, hunting and (for the Sami) herding reindeer, and building igloos as TEMPORARY shelters on the move — not as permanent year-round homes. Their expert understanding of ice, weather and animals, built over thousands of years, is what let them thrive where few others could.
